   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.

|---|---|---|

| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

raw_comment:
The first thing that we can notice is the number of people (60%) who prefer to instantly learn 3 languages. Maybe it is because of a quick correlation that conventional wisdom makes between knowing different languages and overall success. Besides, in comparison with the other skills, I guess it's the only skill that you can apply in different fields of knowledge and different applications, it's less specific than the others. 

The thing I wonder is why people doesn't care about knowing gymnastics. Maybe it's because they do a correlation between exercising and pain/boring stuff, or they think that it is something too easy to master. Or why would people who are (in general) not in any medical related field rather know about neuroscience than reapairing home appliance. Most of these people certainly live in a house and often get struggled by broken stuff.

What did you notice? I noticed that over half of people choose to master three languages of their choice, and the activity with the least amount of people wanting to master is gymnastics.

What do you wonder? Yes, I can understand why more than half the amount of people choose to learn three languages as their top choice because speaking different languages is a super helpful skill that most people should know especially since there are handfuls of people that don't speak English. I also wonder why things like repairing home appliances and oil painting are low on the list because fixing up appliances is way cheaper than paying someone else to do it, and oil painting is super pretty and would be a great skill.

What impact does this have on you and your community? In my neighborhood I have people that don't speak English/English isn't their first language, and I think that being able to learn their language can open up whole new doors for you (like learning about the culture and history)

What's going on in this graph? The big 6 which one would you like to instantly master?

   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

I noticed that each group of circles was designated to a specific skill that a person would master if they could. I wonder why so many people choose to speak three languages of choice, and why so few people choose to master gymnastics. This can impact my community as someone coming from a community where many of the people I know cannot speak three languages but always talk about how they wish they could probably be a big contribution to this graph.

   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.

|---|---|---|

| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |

What do you wonder? What is the difference between neuroscience and psychology or sociology? Why gymnastics?

What impact does this have on you and your community? Not much but from knowing this information, maybe the education system will focus more on the teaching of languages at school?

|---|---|---|

| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |
raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of people would prefer to master skills that they thought would help them be more successful in life, whether it be through being able to communicate with more people (as shown by those who selected being able to speak three languages) or being able to cook for themselves. Far fewer individuals were interested in more creative skills, such as oil painting and gymnastics, hinting that they do not believe there is much to be gained from knowing how to do either of these activities. There does seem to be an overwhelming favor of more "white collar," higher paying jobs, as language fluency and neuroscience would both lead to higher salaries.

I wonder why these were the options. Oil painting seems like a very specific activity, compared to maybe just asking the students if they would want to master just painting. Also, I am curious to see if the students were searching for the "correct" answer or if maybe there was a bias in the polling, as different nationalities or classes might prioritize different skills. As those who participated were subscribers to the New York Times, they might be more interested in more academic activities verses those relating to art, physical education, or home maintenance.

These graph shows what skills high schoolers value, hinting on what classes they will take, degrees they will obtain, and eventually what the job market and the workforce will look like.

"A White Collar Future: America's Upcoming Workforce."

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the majority of those that opted into the survey, 60%, said that they would instantly master three languages of their choice. Directly right after follows 12% of people who said that they would prefer mastering chef skills, and then 11% with neuroscience mastery. 
2. I wonder as to why the gap between mastering three languages and the rest of the skills varies by such a large amount. The difference between 60% and 12% is 48%. I think that this could be because people are just generally interested in immersing themselves in a rich culture that is not their own. Language is the key to understanding people who do not look like you, and great for making connections between one another. 
3. The impact that this would have is having a greater understanding and appreciation for the different cultures that exist in my community. I think that it is so important to understand at least another language because English is not the only language out there with a large amount of speakers.  It would be great to fully understand our differences and how we can make each other smile with the words that we can speak. 
4. In this graph, we get to see the percentages of people who selected a specific skill to instantly master. Catchy headline: "US Priority: To Cook or to Speak?"

   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded!  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Choose Your Skill. Become a Master" by Kaitlin of Massachusetts, “What Quarantine Skill Do You Want to Master?” by Molly of Salt Lake City, “Knock Down Barriers or Enhance Skills: What Would You Choose?” by Destiny of Providence, "Mastering Without Learning: Skills Readers Want Without Practicing" by Olivia of Wisconsin, “Language Fluency Over Gymnastics; Usefulness Over Hobby” by Annalee of Arcata, California, and “The Jack of All Trades Offers You One of His Skills" by Yomi of Minnesota.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Dec. 18 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs). 
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who would love to become a gymnast without accidents and fear, and Kevin DeVizia of Millrift, Pennsylvania, who would love to be able to converse with anyone all over the world, all while developing his mad chef skills.

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |
raw_comment:
By looking at this graph, I notice that majority of the people voting in this poll want to master three languages of choice. In seeing this, I wonder what was the age group of people filling this graph out. One can probably infer that 18+ voted for this skill because of the great opportunities being trilingual could bring a person. This really does not necessarily impact my community as it is just a question about what people would want to master. While mastering 3 languages of choice is the highest, it makes the most sense why. Travel would be easier, working in other countries would be easier, and becoming part of more cultures would be easier. 
New headline, "If so many people want to be trilingual, why aren't they?"

raw_comment: I notice, as most people are noticing, that there is one skill that people would love to master instantly above all others- that skill being to learn three languages of my choice. Above all, I wonder WHY people want to learn other languages. There are other very practical skills on the list, such as repairing home appliances or the ability to cook which would be extremely helpful in every day life, whereas speaking other languages may help occasionally outside of the home (That being said, learning other languages reigned supreme over any other choice). Of course, that is assuming the people who chose the skills were in a place where there first language is the national language. This leads me to my other questions- who was included in the population that took the survey? The impact it has on me as someone who speaks fluently in the language that is most common is probably a deeper consideration of who and why people would love to learn other languages.

raw_comment: In the “What’s Going On In This Graph | December 16, 2020” analyzes the results of an online survey that reflects what skills people choose to master. Our group noticed that there was an abundance of people who would instantly master the skill of knowing three languages of their choice. The graph indicates that 60% of people would want to obtain this skill and the other 40% would prefer to master a different skill. Additionally, our team wonders what three languages the people in the survey would have loved to master. We were also curious why these topics were chosen. Doing gymnastics, mastering languages, repairing home items, etc.. is all very particular and we wonder if there would have been more participants if the topics were more relatable. This impacts our community because most of these skills are basic everyday skills that everyone should learn eventually. It also shows how people would rather be able to communicate better, rather than be knowledgeable in neuroscience. The catchy headline we believe captivates what is going on in this graph would be, “Manifesting a Future Skill.”

raw_comment: After looking at the New York Times graph on which skills people would choose to master instantly we noticed that some of the dots that represented the population are shaded while others are just outlined. We also noticed that a large majority of people surveyed would choose to learn 3 languages. We wonder what these languages would be. Another thing we notice is that gymnastics is the only sport on this list.  We also wonder why people choose the skills they did. This Impacts our community in a positive way because it shows that people are interested in acquiring skills that benefit our community. raw_comment:
The graph is broken down into 100 dots to represent each percent of the 2,250 people surveyed. Each color of the dots corresponds to one of the answer options of the survey. 60% of those surveyed chose to instantly master 3 languages of their choice. The least popular skill to master was gymnastics with only 3% voting for it. 

I wonder why most people chose to learn 3 languages. Did people choose skills that they thought were helpful and applicable to daily life or skills that would be fun to have? I wonder how the skills for the survey were chosen since they're all drastically different and very random when put together. I also wonder who responded to the survey. Are there any trends in the answers based on age, occupation, etc.? 

This impacts me and my community because it shows how many people prioritize communication whether it's personal, for work, or for fun. I think it can also speak to the cultural diversity that our country embraces.

A headline for this graph could be "Choose Your Skill, Become a Master".

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
In this graph, each dot represents 1% of the population taking the poll that generated this data. I notice that 60% of survey takers would choose to instantly master three languages over any other skill. The remaining 40% are split between the following skills: neuroscience, oil painting, repairing any home appliance, and gymnastics. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what was the primary demographic of people taking this survey. Were most over the age of 18? Were most living in areas with people of many cultures? Were many from urban cities? The answers to all these questions impact the results of the data. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This survey shows that the majority of people hope to learn new languages. This data can be used to impact my community because my classmates and I can help co-found a language club that helps expose people to several languages.

|---|---|---|

| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the responses of the New York Times’s research-and-analytics department survey of 2,250 subscribers who chose to participate.  They were asked in this voluntary online survey “Which would you choose to instantly master?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or 
a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs).  
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  This is the last graph of 2020.  The next graph release will be by Friday, Jan. 1, 2021 with moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 6.  Stay tuned for which graph will be posted.

raw_comment: I think it is important to point out that the survey only provided a few options for skills. Of course, giving people completing the survey unlimited options for possible skills would make it difficult to organize responses in a meaningful way, it should be recognized that changing the options for skills could drastically affect the results of the survey. I notice that many of the skills all require a significant time commitment. I wonder if perhaps the survey takers chose the skills because of the time investment they would require. I also wonder if the skills chosen reflect how the survey takers spend their free time (those who chose chef skills having an interest in baking, for example.) This graph could affect my community by showing what skills those in my community will be most likely to invest time in (though of course the results would be more accurate to my community if the survey was conducted entirely inside of it.) If I were to create a headline for this graphic, I would make it say "The Skills People Want."

   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that 60% of people would want to master three languages of their choice which blew the other options out of the water. The next closest option was chef skills which was still only 12%.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why so many people selected to master three languages of their choice. What will they use the mastery of this skill for? Jobs? Communicating with friends? What are the top three languages that people say they would want to master? There are so many different languages in the world, so I wonder what the most popular languages selected were.

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the majority of people would choose to master three languages. I also notice that 11% of people would choose to master neuroscience, which shows me that those people are probably motivated by money. 
2.  I wonder why 8% of people would like to master oil painting? Most of the others are useful to everyday life, but oil painting is not a necessary skill. 
3. This shows me that my community probably does not speak lots of languages because 60% of people want to learn more languages. It also shows me that people in my community may be laking culinary skills. 
4. A catchy headline for this graph is: Americans choose practicality over pleasure.

| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph shows the responses of a survey. This survey gave participants a list of skills and asked them which skill they would choose to instantly master. Learning different languages can not only make travel easier, but it can also help preserve disappearing languages that are important to certain cultures.
